meta.blurb: Marta delivers parcels all day and lies awake at night worrying about money. She decides to write one plan on a single sheet, with a few clear steps, and to keep to it for ten years. It is simple enough to copy.
meta.bible: Marta: a parcel delivery driver aged thirty-eight at the start, practical and a little tired of money worry. Kofi: her younger brother, a student with many questions. Dev: Marta's partner, a school cook, who joins the plan in the second half. The plan: Marta writes it on one page and keeps it for ten years. All money amounts are plain numbers with no currency. The examples (yearly costs of 24,000, a pile of about 600,000) are imagined illustrations, not promises. Key terms: wealth, income, assets, debt, net worth, savings rate, emergency cushion, broad fund, rule of thumb, automate, inflation, withdrawal. A rule of thumb that a pile of about twenty-five times yearly costs may support spending is described as a guide only and not a guarantee. Markets can fall and recover; no returns are promised. Tax and employer plans differ by country. Voice: calm, plain, encouraging and honest. The final beat says this is general information and not financial advice. Added for the full-length book (all imagined): Marta takes home about 2,500 a month, 30,000 a year, and at first spends about 2,400 a month, 28,800 a year. She owes 2,400 on a credit card at about twenty in a hundred a year, and owns about 1,000 in savings, an old car worth about 4,000 and about 1,000 of other things; her net worth at the start is about 3,600. She and Dev move from Harbour Road to a smaller flat on Fern Street, which cuts her share of the rent from 1,000 to 700 and her monthly costs to 2,000, or 24,000 a year. The card is cleared in about nine months; the first cushion is two months of costs, about 4,000, later three months; she keeps fun money and a small family help budget. Her page of lines: know your numbers, spend less than you earn, clear expensive debt, keep a cushion, own the whole basket (one broad, low-cost fund), automate it on payday, and later a seventh line, insure only what could ruin me. Ines: Marta's depot manager at the depot on Dale Road. Bram: a driver at the depot who sells in the crash and regrets it. Mr Hale: a smooth salesman with a commission product. Mrs Pell: a neighbour from Harbour Road who lost savings to a scheme promising a guaranteed return. Tomas: Kofi's friend, who loses most of his savings on a fashionable idea. Mr Aziz: a retired tailor aged seventy-two, a neighbour on Fern Street, who lives on savings. Ms Reyes: a fee-only adviser. Places: the college (Marta's night course in logistics), Brook Park (the bench), Alder School (where Dev cooks). Timeline: year one ends with the card clear, the cushion full and the fund begun, net worth about 9,500; in year two her old car breaks down and the repair costs about 1,100, paid from the cushion; in year three markets fall by about a third and take about two years to recover; in year four she becomes a planner at the depot with a rise of about 3,000 a year after tax; after about six years her savings equal two years of costs; in year seven she works four days a week for a fifth less pay; at the tenth review her fund and cushion total about 90,000, more than three times yearly costs and about a seventh of the way to her target of about 625,000 in today's money. Facts used: a rule of thumb of about twenty-five times yearly costs comes from studies of past markets and is a guide only; saving one in ten might take about fifty years and saving half about seventeen, in an imagined example with modest steady growth; a yearly charge of one in a hundred against one in a thousand can cost tens of thousands over thirty years on 100,000; prices rising three in a hundred a year roughly double in about twenty-four years. Tax, employer plans and insurance differ by country. This is not a book about any one product or company.

beats.scene: Marta sits in her white delivery van at night, parcel list on her knee
beats.summary: Marta, a delivery driver aged thirty-eight, has no plan for her money and lies awake worrying about the future.

beats.scene: Marta carries parcels past rows of different houses in early morning light
beats.summary: On her route she sees homes of every kind and wonders how people afford them, while her own pay vanishes each month.

beats.scene: A phone shows a bank balance close to zero on the last day
beats.summary: Each month her pay arrives and is gone by the end, and the balance is nearly empty again.

beats.scene: A credit card bill with a large interest figure lies on a kitchen table
beats.summary: She pays only the minimum on her credit card each month and feels she is getting nowhere.

beats.scene: Kofi and Dev set out plates while Marta drops her keys by the door
beats.summary: On Sunday her younger brother Kofi, a student, comes to dinner cooked by her partner Dev, a school cook.

beats.scene: Kofi leans across the table asking a question while Marta holds a fork
beats.summary: Kofi asks what wealth really is, and Marta finds she cannot answer.

beats.scene: A big house with a loan sign beside a small flat and a jar
beats.summary: They talk about people who look rich, like a neighbour with a fine house and a huge loan, and Marta wonders whether looking rich is the same as being rich.

beats.scene: A short note on a napkin reads: own, minus owe, equals wealth
beats.summary: Kofi works out the answer: wealth is not income or show but what you own and keep, after what you owe.

beats.scene: Kofi draws three gears labelled earn, keep and grow on a napkin
beats.summary: Wealth grows from three engines working together: earning money, keeping some of it, and making it grow.

beats.scene: A sheet headed my plan lies on the table with six empty lines
beats.summary: Marta decides to write one simple plan on a single page, with a few clear steps, and to keep to it for ten years.

beats.scene: Marta stares at a stack of unopened letters beside a closed laptop
beats.summary: Step one is to know her numbers, and she admits she has avoided them because looking felt frightening.

beats.scene: Bills, a bank statement and a loan letter are spread across the floor
beats.summary: She spreads every bill, statement and letter across the living-room floor, and Dev brings her a mug of tea.

beats.scene: Marta writes her monthly pay at the top of a clean sheet
beats.summary: She starts with what comes in: about 2,500 a month after tax, which is 30,000 a year.

beats.scene: Highlighter lines mark rows of payments on three months of statements
beats.summary: She goes through three months of statements, marking every payment, and finds money leaving in places she had forgotten.

beats.scene: A single credit card balance of 2,400 is circled on a lined sheet
beats.summary: She lists what she owes: a credit card balance of 2,400 charged at a high rate, and nothing else.

beats.scene: Marta lists a small savings account, an old car and some furniture
beats.summary: She lists what she owns: about 1,000 in savings, an old car worth about 4,000, and furniture and other things worth about 1,000.

beats.scene: Marta draws a line under two columns and writes a total
beats.summary: Her net worth, what she owns minus what she owes, is about 3,600: small but real, and it is her starting point.

beats.scene: Marta adds a column of monthly costs and multiplies the total by twelve
beats.summary: She adds up her monthly costs of 2,400 and multiplies by twelve to find her yearly costs: 28,800.

beats.scene: A large circled number, 28,800, stands alone on a notepad
beats.summary: The yearly cost of her life is the number her whole plan will be built around, because it shows the size of the life she is paying for.

beats.scene: Marta falls asleep with the lamp on and a finished sheet beside her
beats.summary: She sees that she saves only about 100 a month, but facts feel calmer than fog, and she sleeps well for the first time in weeks.

beats.scene: Two arrows on a chart: money coming in is longer than money going out
beats.summary: Step two is to spend less than you earn, because the gap between the two is the engine of the whole plan.

beats.scene: Marta writes every coffee and snack in a small notebook for a month
beats.summary: She tracks every purchase for a month and learns that small treats feel big but add up to less than she feared.

beats.scene: Marta circles three big items on a spending list with a green pen
beats.summary: Housing, transport and food make up most of her spending, and cutting them matters far more than counting small daily savings.

beats.scene: A phone screen lists subscriptions while Marta's thumb cancels three of them
beats.summary: She cancels three subscriptions she barely uses, saving about 40 a month, a small win that makes her feel in control.

beats.scene: Dev sits on the sofa with a rent letter, looking thoughtful
beats.summary: She raises the biggest cost with Dev: her share of their rent is 1,000 a month, far more than they need to pay.

beats.scene: Marta and Dev view an empty smaller flat with sunlight on the floor
beats.summary: They look at smaller, cheaper flats closer to Marta's depot, and Dev worries about leaving his neighbours and his big kitchen.

beats.scene: Marta and Dev sign a lease at a desk while a clerk watches
beats.summary: They choose a flat on Fern Street that is smaller but cheaper, cutting Marta's share of the rent from 1,000 to 700.

beats.scene: Marta, Dev and Kofi carry boxes up the stairs of the cheaper flat
beats.summary: On moving day Kofi helps carry boxes up the stairs, and Marta feels that one decision has already paid her a rise.

beats.scene: Dev stirs a big pot while neat food boxes line the counter
beats.summary: Dev, who cooks for hundreds of children, teaches her to cook big batches, so she wastes less food and buys fewer takeaways.

beats.scene: Marta marks a green tick beside a new, smaller total on her page
beats.summary: With the move and a few other changes, her monthly costs fall from 2,400 to 2,000, or 24,000 a year, and a real gap opens.

beats.scene: A thick credit card statement shows one large interest figure in red
beats.summary: Step three is to clear expensive debt, because high interest works against the plan every single month.

beats.scene: A calculator beside a card statement shows forty a month in interest
beats.summary: On a balance of 2,400 at about twenty in a hundred a year, interest costs about 40 a month, and paying only the minimum keeps her stuck for years.

beats.scene: A bucket with a small hole stands under a running tap
beats.summary: Marta thinks of the debt as a bucket with a hole: whatever she pours into savings leaks out through interest.

beats.scene: Kofi frowns over a notebook while Marta taps her calculator
beats.summary: Kofi asks why she does not invest first, and Marta works out that paying off a card at twenty in a hundred is a sure gain that no investment can promise.

beats.scene: A chart on the fridge shows the debt falling in blocks each month
beats.summary: She sends most of her monthly gap to the card and a smaller part to a cushion, and she colours in a block each payday.

beats.scene: Marta passes a shop window full of sale signs, holding her purse shut
beats.summary: A sale tempts her, so she builds a small amount of fun money into the plan, because a plan that allows no joy will not last.

beats.scene: A half-filled chart shows the card balance cut in half
beats.summary: Halfway through, the balance is half as large, the monthly interest is smaller, and she feels the first real proof that the plan works.

beats.scene: Dev hands Marta a letter about his small low-interest loan
beats.summary: Dev has a small loan with a low interest rate, and they agree that cheap, sensible debt can wait while expensive debt goes first.

beats.scene: A calendar with the last debt payment crossed out and a small star
beats.summary: After about nine months the card is paid off, and Marta feels lighter than she has felt in years.

beats.scene: Marta writes a short rule on a card beside her page
beats.summary: She adds a rule to her page: pay any card in full every month, or do not use it, and her page now has three lines.

beats.scene: A broken washing machine leaks onto a kitchen floor beside a credit card
beats.summary: Step four is a cushion, and Marta remembers last year, when a broken washing machine went straight onto the card.

beats.scene: A calendar with two months highlighted beside a notebook sum
beats.summary: She decides the first cushion should cover two months of costs, about 4,000, and that three months is better when income is less steady.

beats.scene: A phone screen shows a savings account labelled cushion with the word safe
beats.summary: The cushion lives in a safe, easy-to-reach account, apart from her investments, so she cannot spend it by accident or watch it fall.

beats.scene: Marta places an envelope marked cushion inside a drawer beside a short list
beats.summary: She writes the rules for the cushion: it is for job loss, urgent repairs and medical bills, never for sales or holidays.

beats.scene: A dentist's chair and a bill of 300 on a clipboard
beats.summary: Her first test comes when a tooth needs urgent treatment, and the cushion pays the 300 without a word of worry.

beats.scene: A small plant and a coin beside a rising price tag
beats.summary: She learns that a cushion earns little interest while prices creep up, so it slowly loses value, and that this is the small price of safety.

beats.scene: A thermometer drawn on the fridge fills slowly with green pen
beats.summary: Dev draws a thermometer on the fridge, and each payday they colour in a little more of the cushion.

beats.scene: Marta stands at the depot gate in the rain, watching quiet lorries
beats.summary: In a quiet season her overtime disappears for weeks, and the cushion lets her stay calm while her pay is thinner.

beats.scene: Dev brings tea to Marta as she looks at a full thermometer
beats.summary: Eleven months in, the cushion reaches its first target, and Marta feels something she did not expect: calm.

beats.scene: Marta writes the fourth line on her page in neat letters
beats.summary: She writes line four, keep two months of costs in cash, and wonders what to do with the money beyond that.

beats.scene: A jar of cash on a shelf beside a rising price tag
beats.summary: Step five is to grow the rest, because cash alone cannot keep up with rising prices over many years.

beats.scene: Kofi draws a small bakery with a tick next to the word share
beats.summary: Kofi explains shares with a bakery: owning a share means owning a small piece of a company and of its future profits.

beats.scene: Marta stares at a wall of company names on a news screen
beats.summary: Marta wonders which companies to pick, but even experts often fail to pick the winners again and again.

beats.scene: A single large basket filled with many different small fruits
beats.summary: A broad fund works like a basket: for a small cost, it holds tiny pieces of hundreds or thousands of companies at once.

beats.scene: A fund card reads low cost beside a long list of companies
beats.summary: An index fund simply follows a long list of companies instead of choosing among them, so its yearly cost can be very small.

beats.scene: Marta compares a long menu of dozens of funds with a single short card
beats.summary: Faced with dozens of funds, she realises that one broad, low-cost fund is enough, and that fewer choices mean fewer mistakes.

beats.scene: A fund fact sheet with a finger resting on the yearly charge line
beats.summary: She reads the fund's papers carefully, checking the yearly charge and what it holds, because no fund can promise a result.

beats.scene: Marta fills in an online form while Dev rests a hand on her shoulder
beats.summary: Opening an account takes an evening of forms and proof of identity, and her hand shakes a little as she presses send.

beats.scene: Marta's finger hovers above a button marked buy on a phone
beats.summary: She buys her first small amount, and the next day the price moves a little, which she shrugs off, because she plans to hold for years.

beats.scene: Marta writes the fifth line, own the whole basket, on her page
beats.summary: Her fifth line says to put the rest into one broad, low-cost fund and leave it alone.

beats.scene: A poster in a hotel lobby offers a free money check evening
beats.summary: A flyer invites Marta to a free money evening, and curiosity leads her to a hotel meeting room.

beats.scene: A man in a smart suit points at a glossy chart across a desk
beats.summary: Mr Hale, a smooth salesman, shows her a glossy product with a clever name that he says will beat the market.

beats.scene: A thick contract with small print and a penalty clause circled
beats.summary: The product has high yearly charges, a heavy penalty if she leaves early, and pages of small print.

beats.scene: Marta asks a question while Mr Hale shifts in his chair
beats.summary: Marta asks how he is paid, and he admits that he earns a commission when she signs.

beats.scene: A card with the words two sentences written in Marta's hand
beats.summary: She makes a rule: if she cannot explain a product in two plain sentences, she does not buy it.

beats.scene: Kofi types numbers into a spreadsheet showing two lines drawing apart
beats.summary: Kofi shows her that a yearly charge of one in a hundred, compared with one in a thousand, can cost tens of thousands over thirty years on a pile of 100,000.

beats.scene: Three questions are written on a card beside a handshake
beats.summary: She writes three questions for anyone selling her money advice: how are you paid, what are all the costs, and what happens if I leave early?

beats.scene: An adviser with a flat-fee card sits at a plain desk
beats.summary: A fee-only adviser, who is paid a flat fee by the customer and not a commission, can be worth hiring for a specific question.

beats.scene: Mrs Pell sits in a kitchen holding an empty envelope
beats.summary: Mrs Pell, a neighbour from the old street, once lost her savings to a scheme that promised a high, guaranteed return.

beats.scene: Marta drops a glossy brochure in a recycling bin and keeps a plain folder
beats.summary: She learns that a promise of high returns with no risk is a warning sign, and she keeps her plain folder.

beats.scene: A long chart line climbs across a century with many dips
beats.summary: Marta studies a chart of a broad market over about a hundred years: it climbs, but never in a straight line.

beats.scene: A bakery counter with queues of customers and a busy till
beats.summary: Over time, companies sell things, earn profits and grow, and owners of shares share in that growth, though never with a promise.

beats.scene: A newspaper headline in black type shows prices falling sharply
beats.summary: Prices also fall, sometimes by a third or more, and that has happened more than once in history.

beats.scene: Kofi holds his hands wide and asks whether everything could vanish
beats.summary: Kofi asks if she could lose everything, and Marta learns that one company can fail while a broad fund of hundreds survives, though a whole market can fall.

beats.scene: A calendar with five years marked in a block beside a coin
beats.summary: Money needed within five years does not belong in the fund; money for the distant future does.

beats.scene: Marta and Dev walk up a hilly road with dips and a long view
beats.summary: On a Sunday walk, Dev says that markets are like the hill road: bumpy underfoot, but climbing over many miles.

beats.scene: Marta imagines a red number on her phone and grips the table
beats.summary: The real danger is not the market but fear: many people sell in a panic at exactly the wrong time.

beats.scene: Marta writes a short rule on a card and tapes it to her fridge
beats.summary: She writes a rule for bad years: do not sell in a panic, and do not look every day.

beats.scene: Dev draws a falling line on paper beside a pretend balance
beats.summary: Dev suggests a rehearsal: imagine the fund losing a third of its value, and decide now what she will do.

beats.scene: Marta switches off price alerts and puts her phone in a drawer
beats.summary: She switches off every price alert and decides to look at her fund no more than once a month.

beats.scene: A diary page shows a saving promise crossed out three months in a row
beats.summary: Step six is to automate, because in her first months Marta moved money by hand and sometimes forgot or gave in.

beats.scene: A phone screen shows a scheduled transfer set for the day after payday
beats.summary: She sets up a transfer for the day after payday, so that saving happens before she can spend.

beats.scene: Two arrows leave a pay slip, to a cushion and a fund
beats.summary: Her payday transfers are set once: part to finish the cushion, then everything to the fund, in the same amounts each month.

beats.scene: Marta looks at a smaller balance on her phone and shrugs
beats.summary: At first the account looks emptier, but she adjusts quickly, because money she does not see is money she does not spend.

beats.scene: Three months of calendar pages ticked with no missed transfer
beats.summary: By the third month she no longer thinks about it, and the plan runs by itself like a clock in the next room.

beats.scene: A staircase of equal coin stacks climbs beside a wavy price line
beats.summary: Investing the same amount every month buys more when prices are low and less when they are high, which is not magic but takes away the guessing.

beats.scene: A tax refund letter lies beside Marta's pen and a phone
beats.summary: When a small tax refund arrives, she sends most of it straight to the plan before it can drift into the shops.

beats.scene: Kofi at a student desk sets up a ten-a-week transfer on his laptop
beats.summary: Kofi, on a student budget, sets up an automatic ten a week, proving that starting small beats waiting.

beats.scene: A calendar page marked January with a small up arrow
beats.summary: She decides to raise her automatic amount a little each January and each time her pay rises.

beats.scene: Marta writes line six, automate it on payday, on her page
beats.summary: Line six is added to her page: make it automatic on payday.

beats.scene: A tall pile of coins stands beside a measuring stick
beats.summary: Marta asks the question that has been hiding in her plan: how big a pile does a person need?

beats.scene: A pile of coins with one small stack being taken away each year
beats.summary: The idea is a pile big enough that selling a small part each year could pay for a life, while the rest keeps growing.

beats.scene: A notepad shows yearly costs with a times twenty-five sign beside it
beats.summary: Some planners use a rule of thumb that a pile of about twenty-five times yearly costs may support spending for decades, but it is a guide and not a guarantee.

beats.scene: Marta writes 24,000 on a notepad and draws an arrow to 600,000
beats.summary: In an imagined example, yearly costs of 24,000 point to a pile of about 600,000.

beats.scene: A page of old market records with a pen tracing thirty-year lines
beats.summary: The rule comes from researchers who studied past markets and found that spending about four in a hundred a year lasted through most past periods, though the future may differ.

beats.scene: Marta looks tiny beneath a huge drawn mountain labelled six hundred thousand
beats.summary: Marta feels dizzy at such a big number, and Dev tells her that nobody climbs a mountain at once, only one steady step after another.

beats.scene: Two paths on a map, one with more steps, both reaching a town
beats.summary: How much of your income you save matters most: saving half of your pay reaches independence far sooner than saving a tenth.

beats.scene: A table of saving shares and years with a note saying imagined
beats.summary: In an imagined example with modest steady growth, saving one in ten may take about fifty years, while saving half may take about seventeen.

beats.scene: Marta crosses out a number on a notepad and writes a smaller one
beats.summary: Cutting yearly costs by 3,000 lowers the target by 75,000 and lifts savings at once, a double gain.

beats.scene: Marta writes a target and a first milestone in the margin of her page
beats.summary: She writes her target in the margin, about 600,000 and maybe less, and her first milestone: two full years of costs.

beats.scene: Kofi points at two arrows on a notepad: costs and income
beats.summary: Kofi points out that costs can only fall so far, while income can rise much further.

beats.scene: Marta lists her skills on a pad: routes, schedules, calm under pressure
beats.summary: Marta lists what she is good at: knowing routes, planning schedules and staying calm when a day goes wrong.

beats.scene: Ines the depot manager points at a poster on a notice board
beats.summary: Ines, her depot manager, mentions a night course in logistics at the college and says it could lead to a planner's job.

beats.scene: Marta studies a night course timetable beside an application form
beats.summary: Marta fills in the application and pays the fee of about 900 in three parts, from a small pot she sets aside for it.

beats.scene: Marta sits at the back of a classroom among students half her age
beats.summary: On the first night she sits among students half her age and feels out of place, until the teacher praises her sensible questions.

beats.scene: Marta rests her head on her books at a kitchen table at midnight
beats.summary: In a tiring week, work, classes and sleep collide, and she nearly quits, but Dev cooks and Kofi quizzes her.

beats.scene: Marta loads parcels into vans at the depot at dawn in the busy season
beats.summary: In the busy season she takes extra shifts, and she sets a rule that every extra coin goes to the plan before it reaches her daily life.

beats.scene: Kofi shows a first tutoring payment on his phone with a grin
beats.summary: Kofi earns his first money tutoring younger pupils and puts part of it into his own small fund.

beats.scene: Marta holds a certificate with a bright ribbon beside Dev and Kofi
beats.summary: Marta passes her first-year exams, and the family celebrates at Dev's favourite cheap restaurant.

beats.scene: Ines points at an empty office desk with a computer and a map
beats.summary: Ines tells her that a planner's job may open in a couple of years, when the course ends, and promises to remember her name.

beats.scene: A leaflet about tax-friendly accounts lies on a desk beside a calculator
beats.summary: Many countries have accounts with tax benefits for retirement or long-term saving, and Marta decides to find out what hers offers.

beats.scene: Marta signs a form at a desk while a clerk hands her a leaflet
beats.summary: At the depot, she learns that the employer adds money when workers save into the retirement plan, and that she has been missing out for years.

beats.scene: A matching coin drops into a jar beside Marta's coin
beats.summary: Taking a match is like being paid extra for saving, so she signs up at once, though details differ from country to country.

beats.scene: A padlock beside a retirement account page with a date on it
beats.summary: She reads the rules: money in such accounts is often locked until later in life, so her cushion stays separate.

beats.scene: Marta reads a government website on a laptop, with an advert closed
beats.summary: Rules and limits change, so she checks official government websites and not adverts.

beats.scene: Marta watches her first yearly statement arrive with a small smile
beats.summary: At the end of year one, her cushion is full, her card is clear, and her fund has begun to grow slowly.

beats.scene: Marta and Dev share tea beside a calendar ringed in January
beats.summary: She makes the yearly review a ritual: one hour, one evening, the same date every year, with tea.

beats.scene: Marta writes a new total under last year's net worth line
beats.summary: Her net worth has grown from about 3,600 to about 9,500 in one year, the best number she has ever written.

beats.scene: Dev reads Marta's page by lamplight and nods slowly
beats.summary: Dev reads her page and says he would like his own numbers looked at, soon.

beats.scene: Kofi yawns beside a pile of plain folders
beats.summary: Kofi says the plan is the most boring thing he has ever seen, and Marta replies that it works precisely because it is boring.

beats.scene: A broken car stands with its bonnet open as a tow truck arrives
beats.summary: In year two, Marta's old car breaks down on the way to her night class, and the repair will cost about 1,100.

beats.scene: Marta's thumb hovers over a credit card app, then moves away
beats.summary: Her old reflex is to reach for a card, but she stops and remembers the cushion.

beats.scene: A mechanic hands Marta a bill while she taps her bank card
beats.summary: She pays the bill from the cushion in full, and the mechanic wonders why she is smiling.

beats.scene: A thermometer on a fridge with the green level lowered by one step
beats.summary: The cushion is lower now, so she makes a rule: refill the cushion first, before any new money goes to the fund.

beats.scene: Marta weighs repair costs on a kitchen scale beside a car key
beats.summary: She also learns a rule: when a repair costs more than half the car's value, stop and think about replacing it.

beats.scene: Kofi sits with a cracked phone and a worried look at the table
beats.summary: Kofi, short of rent, asks for help, and Marta lends a small amount from her fun money, not from her cushion or her fund.

beats.scene: Marta writes a family help line at the bottom of her fun money budget
beats.summary: She adds a small budget for helping family, so that generosity does not break the plan.

beats.scene: Dev opens a new account labelled cushion with a careful smile
beats.summary: Seeing how calm Marta was, Dev starts his own cushion by putting aside a little each payday.

beats.scene: A statement shows an extra line of money from the depot's matching plan
beats.summary: The employer's match appears on her statement as a separate line, and Marta feels the thrill of free money.

beats.scene: Marta writes a short note in the margin of her page
beats.summary: At the end of year two, her plan has survived its first shock, and she writes a note in the margin: refill the cushion first.

beats.scene: News screens in a depot canteen show grim headlines and falling numbers
beats.summary: In year three, grim headlines fill the news, and prices fall across the markets.

beats.scene: A fund statement shows a red number while Marta sits very still
beats.summary: In this imagined crash, her fund falls by about a third in a few months, and her stomach tightens.

beats.scene: Colleagues in the canteen whisper over their phones
beats.summary: At the depot, colleagues talk of selling everything, and her friend Bram says he will sell at once.

beats.scene: Marta reads the card on her fridge while Dev holds her hand
beats.summary: She reads her card, talks to Dev, and decides to do nothing.

beats.scene: A full cushion thermometer sits next to a fund statement in red
beats.summary: Because her cushion is full and her job is steady, she has no need to sell anything, which is the cushion's other job: it lets the fund stay put.

beats.scene: Marta raises her automatic transfer slightly, with a nervous smile

beats.scene: Marta stands relaxed on a balcony with a mug, watching rain

beats.scene: Marta writes a short note at the bottom of her page
beats.summary: No plan can promise what markets will do or how laws will change, but a plan is better than worry.

B1B2: Marta is thirty-eight, and she delivers parcels all day in a small white van. She earns a steady wage, but she has no plan for her money, and at night she lies awake and worries.
On her route Marta sees small flats, big houses and everything between them. She wonders how all these people pay for their lives, while her own pay seems to disappear every month.
Her pay arrives on the last day of the month, and by the twentieth there is almost nothing left. She checks her phone, sees the same small number again, and puts it away with a sigh.
Her credit card bill arrives with a large number for interest printed in red. She pays the smallest amount allowed, and the balance hardly moves.
On Sunday evenings her brother Kofi comes to eat, and Dev, who cooks for a school all week, makes dinner anyway. Kofi is a student with a bag full of books and a head full of questions.
Between mouthfuls, Kofi asks what wealth really is, and he wants a real answer, not a slogan. Marta opens her mouth, closes it again, and realises she has never thought about it.
They talk about a neighbour who has a huge house, two shiny cars and a very large loan. Marta wonders whether looking rich is really the same as being rich.
Kofi thinks for a moment and writes on a napkin: what you own, minus what you owe. Wealth, he says, is not how much you earn or how rich you look, but what you really keep.
Kofi draws three gears that turn together and labels them earn, keep and grow. If one gear is missing, he explains, the other two cannot do the whole job.
That night, Marta takes a clean sheet of paper and writes my plan across the top. She promises that it will be simple, that it will fit on one page, and that she will follow it for ten years.
Step one on her page says: know your numbers. Marta has avoided them for years, because looking at a problem feels worse than not looking at it.
On Saturday morning she spreads every bill, statement and letter across the living-room floor. Dev brings her a mug of tea and a plate of toast, and then he wisely leaves her alone.
She begins with the easiest line of all, which is the money that comes in each month. After tax she takes home about 2,500 a month, which makes 30,000 over a year.
Next she goes through three months of bank statements and marks every single payment. Some of them surprise her, because money has been leaving in places she had completely forgotten.
Next she lists what she owes, and the list is short. There is the credit card, with a balance of 2,400 and a high rate of interest, and nothing else.

Then she turns the page and lists everything that she owns, from her small savings to her old sofa. There is about 1,000 in savings, an old car worth about 4,000, and furniture and other things worth about 1,000.
She draws a line under both columns and subtracts what she owes from what she owns. The answer is called net worth, and at about 3,600 it is small but real, a starting point.
Next she adds up all her monthly costs, which come to 2,400. Multiplied by twelve, that gives her yearly costs of 28,800, a number she has never seen before.
Her plan will be built around this yearly number, because it shows the true size of her life. Everything else, from how much to save to how much she needs one day, grows from it.
She sees that she saves only about 100 a month, which is not much. Even so, facts feel calmer than fog, and she sleeps well that night for the first time in weeks.
Step two is simple to say and hard to do: spend less than you earn. Marta draws two arrows, and the gap between them, she sees, is the engine that drives the whole plan.
For one month she writes down everything she buys, even a coffee or a snack. Small treats feel large at the time, but the total is smaller than she feared.
Marta circles her three biggest costs in green: housing, transport and food. Together they swallow most of her money, and they matter far more than any small daily saving.
She finds three subscriptions that she almost never uses and cancels them with a few taps. They cost about 40 a month together, and the small win makes her feel in control.
Then she raises the biggest cost of all with Dev. Her share of the rent is 1,000 a month, which she suspects is more than they really need to pay.
Over several weekends they look at smaller flats that are closer to Marta's depot. Dev worries about leaving his friendly neighbours and his big kitchen, and Marta understands.
They choose a small, bright flat on Fern Street, close to the depot. It costs far less, and Marta's share of the rent drops from 1,000 to 700.
On moving day Kofi carries boxes up the stairs, grumbling cheerfully with every step. Marta looks around the smaller rooms and feels that one decision has already paid her a rise.
Dev cooks for hundreds of children every day, so he teaches Marta to cook big batches. They waste less food, buy fewer takeaways, and eat better for less money.
With the move and a few other changes, her monthly costs fall from 2,400 to 2,000. That makes 24,000 a year, and now a real gap opens between what she earns and what she spends.
Step three is to clear expensive debt, because high interest works against her every single month. Marta looks at her credit card statement under the lamp and sees the interest figure in red.
On a balance of 2,400 at about twenty in a hundred a year, interest costs her about 40 a month. If she pays only the minimum, she will stay stuck in debt for years.
Marta thinks of the debt as a bucket with a hole in the bottom. Whatever she pours into savings leaks out again through the interest, so she must fix the hole first.
Kofi asks why she does not invest first and let the card wait. Marta works out that clearing a card charging twenty in a hundred is a sure gain that no investment can promise.
She sends most of her monthly gap to the card and a smaller part to a cushion. On the fridge, she colours in one block of the debt chart every payday.
A big sale in a shop window tempts Marta, so she builds a little fun money into the plan. A plan that allows no joy at all, she decides, will not last long.
Halfway through, the card balance is half as large, and the monthly interest is smaller too. Marta feels the first real proof that the plan is working.
Dev has a small loan with a very low rate of interest, and he asks if they should rush to pay it. They agree that cheap, sensible debt can wait while the expensive debt goes first.
After about nine months, the last payment goes through and the card balance is zero. Marta feels lighter than she has felt in years, as if she had put down a heavy bag.
She adds a new rule to her page: pay any card in full every month, or do not use it at all. Her page now has three clear lines, and she can feel each one doing its job.
Step four is a cushion, and Marta remembers last year, when a broken washing machine went straight onto her card. A single surprise bill, she sees, can undo many months of good work in one afternoon.
She decides that her first cushion should cover two months of costs, about 4,000. Three months is better when income is less steady, so she plans to grow it later.
The cushion lives in a safe, easy-to-reach account, apart from her investments. That way she cannot spend it by accident, and she does not have to watch it rise and fall.
